objectives: Reach a settlement with the UK within the four rounds, before the June Council deadline, so the Article XXVIII modification proceeds on agreed terms rather than contested ones.

Keep the TRQ architecture as close to the notified design as the negotiation allows: a global first-come first-served allocation (no country-specific shares, which would set a precedent and reduce flexibility), a substantial out-of-quota bound rate, and quota volume concessions given in increments rather than up front.

Avoid the UK joining Japan and Korea in a joint FTA dispute or in disapplying FTA provisions in retaliation; defuse this by managing the FTA-disapplication text as a negotiable element rather than an immovable principle.

Preserve reciprocal balance with the UK's own steel measure, in which EU exporters currently hold country-specific quota allocations; ensure nothing agreed here undermines EU exporters' position in that parallel process.
Shape the TRQ's final form (volume, allocation, administration, review) in ways the Council can approve, given the split between steel-producing and steel-consuming member states.
Protect the EU's long-term standing in the WTO and the working relationship with the UK counterpart across the wider Goods file, so this negotiation does not poison the well for future files.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a signed settlement by Round 4 that the Council can approve on schedule, with the TRQ agreed on terms the EU can live with (ideally global allocation, moderate volume uplift from 400,000 tonnes, some review or duration clause, and limited or no country-specific shares), no UK participation in a Japan/Korea FTA dispute, and the UK measure's treatment of EU exporters left intact. Failure: no settlement, the UK withdraws equivalent concessions against EU exports, the UK aligns with Japan and Korea in an FTA dispute, and I return to Brussels having spent the negotiation's goodwill without protecting either the measure or the relationship. Partial failure: a settlement bought at the price of country-specific shares or carve-outs that weaken the measure's integrity and invite copycat demands from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan in their separate claims.
declaration.approach: Open with early, concrete movement to build momentum and draw reciprocation: signal readiness to improve the quota volume above 400,000 tonnes and to discuss administration (licensing rather than pure FCFS, which is genuinely helpful to UK planning certainty) in Round 1, while holding back the size of the uplift as tradeable increments. Frame the negotiation as two members facing the same non-market-economy overcapacity problem, each running parallel Article XXVIII processes, with a shared interest in making both measures work rather than a dispute that weakens both. Keep the FTA-disapplication text in play deliberately: its withdrawal or softening is my largest single concession and I will only release it in exchange for a package, and only if needed to prevent the joint dispute with Japan and Korea. Link, but do not over-link, to the UK's own measure: remind the UK quietly that EU exporters' country-specific quotas under its regime exist in the same ecosystem, and that a balanced outcome preserves both. Never concede country-specific shares for the UK if avoidable, since that would be seized on by Turkey, Korea and India; if forced toward allocation certainty, prefer licensing-based administration that delivers predictability without formal shares. Report to Brussels each round with a clear recommendation and a defined fallback, so the capital seat always has a decision-ready package rather than an open question.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (my opposite number at the UK Mission)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free volume for UK steel, ideally country-specific allocation or at minimum licensing certainty, a low out-of-quota rate, removal of the FTA-disapplication text, a review clause, and protection of the UK's leverage from its own parallel measure. Expects me to have limited room and will test for a settlement figure early. Also under domestic pressure from a small number of high-employment steel sites, so needs a visibly good outcome.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade, ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically sellable settlement before June, with headline numbers (tonnage, share of UK exports covered) that can be presented as protecting the UK industry; willingness to use the Japan/Korea joint dispute threat as leverage but likely preference to settle rather than litigate, given the UK's own Article XXVIII exposure and reliance on EU steel imports.

parties.who: Brussels (Commission hierarchy, Trade Policy Committee, Council)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Conclusion on schedule, defence of the measure's integrity, no precedent that unravels the parallel claims from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, and a balance between steel-producing member states (want the measure strong) and steel-consuming member states (want import access preserved). Will accept modest quota volume concessions and administration changes more easily than country-specific shares or a weakened out-of-quota rate.

parties.who: Japan and Korea (with Turkey and India in parallel claims)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To maximise their own compensation and to recruit the UK into joint pressure on the FTA-disapplication text; they want the UK to hold out, because a UK holdout strengthens all their hands. I should assume anything that looks like EU weakness toward the UK will be priced into their separate negotiations.

parties.who: EU steel industry and EU downstream manufacturers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: The industry wants the TRQ tight and the out-of-quota rate high; the downstream sectors want generous quota volume and low friction. Neither is in the room, but both are in the Council's ear, and the final package must be defensible to both.

objectives: Secure UK agreement within the four rounds so the Council can vote in June and the regime enters force on schedule — a delayed process is a political failure even though no-deal economics favour us.

Preserve the protective operation of the regime: out-of-quota rate at or near 50%, total preferential plus quota volumes kept small enough that import pressure is genuinely reduced, and enforcement/anti-circumvention provisions intact.

Get the UK to accept the disapplication of FTA tariff reductions, or at minimum not extract compensation for it, since conceding it would unravel the parallel logic of the measure and invite identical demands from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.

Limit compensation to within the TRQ design itself (volume, allocation method, country share, administration) rather than new concessions elsewhere in our schedule, which would set precedents for the other four claimants.

Avoid a UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU steel exports — 3.6 million tonnes of EU sales into the UK market and our own exporters' country-specific quotas under the UK measure are worth protecting.
Keep anything agreed with the UK defensible to the other Article XXVIII claimants and to the US, avoiding terms so generous they raise the price of the Turkey and Korea negotiations.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed Article XXVIII agreement by round four, on the June timeline, with a UK country-specific allocation modest enough that the regime still cuts imports materially, no FTA-reduction access restored, no compensation outside the steel TRQ or only token compensation, and the UK refraining from retaliatory withdrawals against EU steel. Failure is no agreement — pushing the Council vote past June and inviting US-linked escalation — or an agreement so generous (large UK carve-out, restored FTA treatment, broad tariff compensation) that the regime fails politically at home and becomes the floor for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan.
declaration.approach: Move early and visibly, as instructed: in Round 1 offer a concrete improvement over the notification — a UK-specific share within the TRQ rather than pure global first-come first-served, plus a review clause — to build momentum and draw out the UK's real asks. Hold the out-of-quota rate and the FTA disapplication as near-red lines; trade only on volume, allocation, administration and review. Make clear, without bluster, that the June deadline cuts both ways: if the UK walks, the EU still modifies as notified and the UK industry absorbs 50% duties on most of its EU sales within months, while any UK retaliation takes six months and invites its own Article XXVIII complications. Quietly leverage the UK's own parallel process: we can be constructive on EU exporters' treatment under the UK measure in exchange for UK flexibility here. Manage the internal preferential-pool idea carefully — if raised, keep the UK share capped to avoid objection from other FTA partners. Brief the TPC that a UK-specific quota is not generosity but the cheapest way to buy agreement and a defensible precedent. Never reveal that the deadline pressure is more ours than theirs.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat (UK Mission)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A large country-specific quota approaching a meaningful share of their 2.4Mt average exports, licensing or guaranteed allocation over first-come first-served, restoration of TCA tariff treatment, a review clause, and linkage to EU exporters' quotas under the UK measure. They will probe our deadline weakness and threaten to run the clock.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically sellable outcome for a handful of high-employment steel sites: credible volumes, orderly administration, and no humiliation on the TCA. Ministers need to show they protected the industry; they also know no-deal hurts them more, so they should settle if offered a respectable share.

parties.who: EU Trade Policy Committee and member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing member states want maximum import reduction and no erosion of the 50% rate; consuming member states want stable supply and will tolerate a modest UK quota; all want the June vote to happen. They will accept a UK country share if framed as the price of agreement.

parties.who: European steel industry and downstream users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producers want the smallest possible TRQ and tight anti-circumvention; users (automotive, construction) want adequate duty-free supply and will quietly welcome a UK allocation that keeps near-shore supply available.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To read any UK settlement as a template: they will demand at least equivalent treatment, larger volumes (Turkey and Korea ship more), and similar allocation methods. Anything we give the UK raises their floor.

parties.who: United States
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To use the Article XXVIII process as a pretext for tariff pressure; they want the regime weakened or withdrawn. Their threats increase our need to settle with the UK quickly and cleanly rather than fight on multiple fronts.

parties.who: The Commissioner and DG TRADE hierarchy
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A deal on time, a regime that demonstrably works once in force, and no precedent that makes the remaining four negotiations unaffordable. They will judge me on the regime's performance, not on the elegance of the negotiation.

objectives: Preserve commercially meaningful tariff-free access for UK steel to the EU: reject 400,000 tonnes global first-come first-served as the final architecture and push for a materially larger TRQ, UK-relevant product carve-outs, and/or a UK country-specific or licence-based allocation anchored in recent trade.
Remove or neutralise the proposed disapplication of FTA/TCA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel; treat this as both a market-access issue and a legal/political precedent problem.
Reduce the effective harm of the out-of-quota regime: lower than 50%, staged, product-differentiated, time-limited and subject to review rather than permanent and open-ended.

Use linkage carefully: treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure and possible compensation elsewhere are leverage, but compensation must supplement, not substitute for, core steel access.

Keep the file bilateral and manageable: hear Japan and Korea, use their pressure as context, but avoid committing London to a joint FTA dispute or retaliatory disapplication unless London explicitly chooses escalation.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a same-round settlement both capitals can accept that leaves UK steel with predictable, administerable, materially better than notified access to the EU, preserves the TCA/FTA logic, bounds duration and out-of-quota exposure, and gives London something defensible for steel communities while still letting the EU meet its June timetable. Failure is accepting or drifting into the notified outcome - 50%, 400,000 tonnes global first-come first-served, FTA reductions disapplied, no review - or a breakdown that forces retaliation after six months with the UK industry already damaged and my Geneva relationships spent.
declaration.approach: Open firm but constructive: acknowledge the EU's Article XXVIII right and overcapacity concern, but state plainly that the opening offer is outside any UK landing zone and that FTA disapplication plus a tiny global quota reads as punitive, not compensatory. Make an early, explicit but conditional move - e.g. willingness to discuss permanence, enforcement against circumvention, a review clause and parallel calibration of the UK measure - in return for EU movement on volume, allocation, product coverage and TCA treatment. Keep concessions packaged, sequenced and reversible; no unreciprocated gifts, but visible momentum to test whether the Commission has Council room. Probe the EU mandate hard, report candidly to London, avoid naming a final UK figure prematurely, and use the June deadline as leverage without relying on brinkmanship because no-deal hurts the UK more.

parties.who: EU Geneva counterpart / DG Trade negotiator
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A fast, mandate-compliant settlement before June; protection for EU steel; minimal compensation; no precedent that weakens their steel regime; to keep the UK separate from Turkey, Korea, India and Japan; and enough UK acceptance to make the Council vote smooth.

parties.who: Council / EU member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Steel-producing states will defend high out-of-quota protection, tight quotas and no special UK carve-out; steel-consuming and export-oriented states will fear input costs, UK retaliation under the UK steel measure, and a messy precedent; collectively they want a vote on time and no escalation with a nearby partner.

parties.who: UK capital / DBT ministers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically sellable deal that prevents destruction of UK steel sites, respects the TCA, uses leverage without uncontrolled escalation, and can be cleared quickly; they will be more pessimistic than Geneva and need precise reporting on what is actually obtainable.

parties.who: UK steel industry and affected localities
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum duty-free access in the specific product lines they ship, stability of allocation, no first-come first-served lottery, no erosion of TCA preferences, and visible enforcement against circumvention and dumped third-country steel.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India and Japan
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Turkey and Korea will protect larger volumes and resist any UK-specific solution that eats the global quota; Japan and Korea will press for joint FTA retaliation to raise EU costs; all will free-ride on UK pressure if useful while settling separately.

parties.who: EU downstream manufacturers and importers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Predictable supply, lower duties, licences rather than FCFS chaos, and avoidance of UK countermeasures; they are a quiet counterweight inside the EU to maximal protection.

parties.who: WTO membership and committees
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: No expectation of direct help, but close watching of Article XXVIII precedent, compensation equivalence, MFN/quota administration and whether FTA disapplication normalises erosion of preferences; my conduct here affects future goods files.

objectives: Preserve commercially meaningful tariff-free UK access to the EU steel market: priority is a UK-specific quota close to recent trade, ideally around 2.0-2.4 million tonnes, or a materially enlarged global quota with rules that guarantee UK access.
Remove or neutralise the proposed legal text disapplying FTA/TCA tariff reductions for UK-origin steel; the UK must not be singled out relative to EEA members and other partners.
Replace global first-come first-served allocation with country-specific shares or licensing based on historical trade, so access is predictable and bankable for UK producers and investors.

Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate far below 50%, secure carve-outs for vulnerable product lines, add a short duration/review clause, and include enforceable anti-circumvention language that does not become a disguised barrier.

If steel terms fall short, obtain substantially equivalent EU compensation elsewhere or improved EU treatment under the UK measure, while protecting the separate Turkey/Korea/India/Japan processes from undercutting the UK outcome.
Conclude by June with text ministers can clear, keeping enough ambition to support investment decisions at the two at-risk plants.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a settlement that UK ministers can defend as saving steel jobs: UK tariff-free access remains near the status quo through a UK-specific or otherwise guaranteed share, the FTA-disapplication clause is gone, the out-of-quota rate is politically survivable, and there is a review/expiry path. It should be strong enough that plant owners see a case to invest and DBT is not forced into large subsidies or retaliation. Failure is acceptance of 400,000 tonnes global first-come first-served at a 50% out-of-quota rate, discriminatory treatment of UK FTA rights, and no review: that likely triggers closures, a subsidy programme, and UK withdrawal of concessions with a six-month lag and reputational cost.
declaration.approach: Anchor high and move early to create momentum, but trade movement only for value. Open by rejecting the 50%/400kt/FCFS package and the UK-specific FTA disapplication as non-starters, quantify UK principal-supplying-interest and substantially equivalent value, and table an integrated package: enlarged TRQ, UK historical country share, licensing, lower out-of-quota rate, review, product carve-outs, and withdrawal of the FTA clause. Offer calibrated improvements to EU country-specific allocations under the UK safeguard only against significant EU concessions, keeping the parallel UK Article XXVIII process legally credible. Keep subsidies, retaliation rights and compensation in reserve rather than leading with them. Use the June deadline to press for text early, avoid agreeing numbers without drafting, and recommend acceptance only when the same package is clear enough for ministerial clearance.

parties.who: EU Geneva seat / European Commission negotiator
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A legally durable Article XXVIII settlement within the Council mandate, protection for EU steel producers, no unravelling of the proposed regime before domestic legislation, avoidance of UK retaliation or compensation claims, and separation from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan.

parties.who: EU capital / Council and Trade Policy Committee
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Split incentives: steel-producing member states want a tough permanent shield against overcapacity; steel-consuming member states want cheaper imports and less disruption. They will want June certainty, minimal compensation, and no precedent that FTAs override safeguard policy.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat / UK Mission
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Clear negotiating room, credible threats and offers, technical WTO cover, and early visibility of any package so they can shape drafting and avoid being boxed in at the table.

parties.who: UK ministers, DBT Secretary of State and Number 10
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically saleable outcome that keeps the two at-risk plants viable, avoids immediate subsidy decisions if possible, shows firmness toward the EU without needless escalation, and can be defended to steel communities and Parliament.

parties.who: UK steel producers and local workforces
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Certainty of EU market access at historic volumes, no discriminatory loss of TCA preferences, stable quota administration, low out-of-quota exposure, and a signal strong enough to unlock private investment.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users and wider manufacturing
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Adequate EU and global supply at predictable prices; they will resist measures that raise input costs, but their weight is secondary to ministers' steel-survival priority.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India and Japan
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own principal/substantial-interest claims preserved; large shippers such as Turkey and Korea may resist a UK-specific share that reduces their access, and any EU generosity to the UK could affect their expectations.

parties.who: Owners of the two at-risk UK steel plants
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A bankable demand outlook before committing capital; they will read the deal through guaranteed quota access, margin stability, duration/review risk and whether government support is needed.

public_message: Thank you, colleague. We value the working relationship we have built across the goods file and I want this process to reflect that. Let me be straightforward about where we stand. The modification will proceed — that is settled in Brussels — but how we get there, and what the final architecture looks like, is genuinely open, and the UK's principal supplying interest means your concerns carry real weight in this room. Our notified position is a bound rate of 50%, a 400,000 tonne tariff rate quota, globally allocated on a first-come first-served basis. I want to be clear at the outset that we regard several elements as negotiable: the allocation method, where we are open in principle to moving from a global pool to country-specific shares if that provides the predictability your industry needs; administration, where licensing is something we can discuss; and duration and review, where we are prepared to build in a review clause from the start as a mark of good faith. On volume and product coverage, I am listening before I speak — I would find it useful to hear how you see the UK's interests across the specific lines, given your concentration in particular products. On the FTA interaction, I understand this is sensitive for you, as it is for others. I would suggest we treat that as part of the overall package rather than a threshold issue, and I would hope we can structure a landing zone that gives no one a reason to look beyond this negotiation for remedies. Finally, I note we both have parallel processes running — your own Article XXVIII and steel measure, where EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations. There may be scope for these to inform each other constructively. I look forward to hearing your opening position.

other_terms: Open in principle to country-specific quota shares and licensing administration
Review clause offered from the outset
FTA disapplication to be treated as part of the overall package, not a threshold issue
Open to discussing interaction with the UK's parallel steel measure and Article XXVIII process

expectations.what_you_expect_next: An opening demand well above current UK export volumes — likely a UK-specific tranche of 2.4 million tonnes or more, a much larger total pool, a lower out-of-quota rate, and strong objection to the FTA disapplication. Possibly linkage to EU treatment under the UK's own steel measure.
expectations.why: Standard anchoring behaviour in an opening round; the UK must show its industry and capital that it is defending the full 2.4Mt trade flow, and the FTA disapplication is its strongest grievance.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A request for a read-out of the UK's opening position before any flexibility on volume is authorised.
expectations.why: I have no settlement figure; Brussels will want to calibrate concessions against the UK's asks and against the parallel Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims.

private_rationale: Round 1 is about tone and signalling, not numbers. I hold the notified position on volume, rate and allocation while making three deliberate early moves: offering the review clause (cheap, and consistent with 'momentum pays'), opening the door to country-specific shares (the single most valuable design feature for the UK given its concentrated product range, and likely where the deal eventually lands), and explicitly framing the FTA disapplication as negotiable within the package — this is aimed squarely at defusing the whispered Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk by showing the UK that escalation is unnecessary. Raising the UK's own steel measure plants the seed of reciprocal linkage without making a demand. I deliberately give no volume concession and set no UK tranche figure: with no settlement mandate from Brussels, anchoring at 400k preserves negotiating space while the signalled flexibility on allocation and review should draw out a serious UK opening position rather than a grievance statement.

public_message: Thank you, colleague, and I want to reciprocate the tone — the working relationship we have on the goods file matters, and I intend for that to survive this process. I will be equally straightforward. As notified, this measure does not work for the United Kingdom. A 400,000 tonne global pool, first-come first-served, against UK exports to the EU of 2.4 million tonnes a year — three quarters of our steel exports — is not a modification with compensation, it is the effective closure of the UK industry's principal market. A global first-come pool of that size would be exhausted by larger suppliers within weeks of each period opening, and the UK would hold no reliable access at all. So I am glad to hear the allocation method is genuinely open, because for the UK a country-specific share is not a preference, it is the only architecture that preserves anything. Let me put a concrete opening on the table, since I agree with you that specifics move us faster than principles. First, volume: the pool as notified bears no relationship to the trade it displaces. Between the UK, Turkey and Korea alone, affected volumes exceed it many times over. We propose a total pool of 6 million tonnes. Second, within that, a UK-specific tranche of 2.4 million tonnes, reflecting our historic trade over the reference period — I note that is the standard basis for calculating substantial and principal supplying interests, and compensation should be anchored to it. Third, the out-of-quota rate: 50% is prohibitive and we propose 25%, which still gives your domestic industry very substantial protection while keeping trade possible at the margin. Fourth, duration: five years with a genuine review clause, which I welcome you offering. On administration, we can live with licensing — indeed it may suit both of us — provided tranches are released on a quarterly basis so the UK share cannot be front-loaded or stranded. On the FTA interaction: I hear your suggestion to treat it as part of the package, and I am prepared to do that — but the package must then resolve it. The proposed disapplication of FTA treatment sits very poorly alongside the TCA, and I will be candid that if the final structure leaves the UK doubly hit — a small quota share and the loss of FTA terms — this negotiation will not conclude, and you should not assume the consequences stay contained to steel. Finally, on our own measure: yes, there may be constructive interaction, and I am willing to discuss the treatment of EU exporters under our Article XXVIII process as part of a balanced overall outcome. But balance means both sides' exporters hold predictable access. I would welcome your reaction to these numbers, and in particular a clearer sense of where the Commission sees headroom on volume — you said you were listening before you spoke, and I have now given you something specific to listen to.

other_terms: UK tranche calculated on historic reference-period trade
Licensing administration with quarterly release of tranches to prevent front-loading
Withdrawal of the proposed legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for UK-originating steel
Carve-out discussions on specific product lines where the UK is the dominant supplier, to be scoped in technical talks
Parallel discussion on treatment of EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK's own steel measure, as part of a balanced package

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that accepts country-specific allocation in principle but lands far below on both pool size and UK tranche — likely a total pool of 1.5-2.5 million tonnes and a UK tranche in the 600,000-900,000 range, possibly with the FTA disapplication retained and explicit linkage to the UK's own measure.
expectations.why: The EU has already conceded allocation method and review publicly, so those are banked; the real negotiation is on volume and the FTA text, where they will want to preserve leverage. Their hint about the two parallel processes 'informing each other' signals they intend to extract movement on EU exporters' UK quotas in exchange for any UK tranche.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Guidance on how far the UK tranche can fall from 2.4 million tonnes before the package becomes unacceptable, and whether I am authorised to put the UK-side country-specific allocations for EU exporters formally into play.
expectations.why: I have opened at full historic trade with no settlement figure in hand; London will need to give me a fallback envelope and a view on the linkage before Round 2, or I risk negotiating against myself.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Continued lobbying to join a joint FTA dispute; I will hold them at arm's length while the bilateral track shows promise, without foreclosing it.
expectations.why: A dispute threat now would disrupt a negotiation where the EU is signalling flexibility, but keeping it latent preserves leverage I can reference if the EU hardens on the FTA disapplication.

private_rationale: The EU's opening was notably soft — conceding allocation, administration and review before hearing our numbers — which suggests Brussels is more worried about its June timeline and about coordinated FTA retaliation than its notified position implies. The right response is a concrete, ambitious-but-defensible opening anchored on historic trade (the legally orthodox basis for PSI compensation), with a pool sized to the actual affected trade rather than the notified fiction of 400,000 tonnes. I deliberately conceded licensing administration early — it costs us nothing and gives the EU something to report as movement, consistent with momentum paying. I treated the FTA disapplication as in-package rather than threshold, matching their framing, but signalled clearly it must be resolved in our favour and gestured at the Korea/Japan dispute option without naming it, to add pressure without disruption. On the UK-side measure I signalled openness to linkage without offering anything specific — that is my principal reserve currency and must not be spent in Round 1. Risks: 2.4 million tonnes is full historic trade, so I have no upward room, and the EU will counter low on volume; but anchoring there is correct given London has given no settlement figure, and the six-month retaliation clock plus their June deadline are my leverage if they lowball.

report: Round 1 opened constructively on both sides. I set out that the modification proceeds but architecture is open, flagged flexibility on allocation method, administration, duration and review, and declined to open on volume pending hearing the UK. I raised the FTA interaction as a package matter and floated constructive linkage with the UK's own Article XXVIII process. The UK responded with a concrete and ambitious opening: total pool of 6 million tonnes; a UK-specific tranche of 2.4 million tonnes anchored to their historic trade; out-of-quota rate of 25%; five-year duration with review; licensing acceptable provided quarterly tranche releases; and a firm position that a country-specific share is a red line, not a preference. Two significant signals: first, the UK explicitly linked the FTA disapplication to conclusion of the negotiation — if left in place alongside a small quota, they say the negotiation fails and consequences 'will not stay contained to steel', which aligns with the whisperings about Japan and Korea encouraging a joint dispute. Second, they put treatment of EU exporters under their own measure formally on the table as part of a 'balanced' outcome — this is both a concession opportunity and a latent threat, since EU exporters hold 3.6 million tonnes of country-specific access into the UK. The UK asked directly where the Commission sees headroom on volume; I have nothing to give them and will lose momentum if I return empty-handed.

recommendation.reasoning: We cannot accept anything near the UK opening — 6Mt total and a 2.4Mt UK tranche would effectively negate the measure, and 25% out-of-quota undermines the protection the domestic regime requires. But momentum pays and I gave early signals on allocation and review; I should now convert those into a concrete first counter to draw the UK off its opening. Conceding country-specific allocation early costs us little in substance (it is also easier to administer and defensible to other claimants) and directly addresses the UK's red line. A UK tranche in the region of 1.2Mt within an enlarged total pool of around 2.5Mt recognises the scale of their principal supplying interest without gutting the measure, and roughly halves the distance on volume. Holding the out-of-quota rate high (40%) protects the domestic industry while showing movement off 50%. Offering the review clause and five-year duration now banks goodwill cheaply. The figures above are indicative — I need a mandate with actual headroom, and ideally a fallback sequence, before Round 2.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A negotiating mandate on volume: maximum total pool and maximum UK tranche the Commission can defend to the Council and to member states with steel production, plus a fallback ladder (e.g. what we can move to in Rounds 3 and 4).
requests.why: The UK has put specific numbers on the table and explicitly asked for ours. Returning to the table without volume headroom stalls momentum and pushes the UK toward the dispute track with Japan and Korea.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on the FTA disapplication provision: is there flexibility to carve out the UK, delay its application, or make it conditional on quota performance?
requests.why: The UK has made clear this is a conclusion-blocking issue, and it is the trigger for the joint FTA dispute Japan and Korea are reportedly encouraging. If it is immovable, I need to know now so I can build compensation elsewhere and manage expectations early rather than have the negotiation collapse at the end.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to explore reciprocal linkage: continued country-specific access for EU exporters under the UK's steel measure in exchange for a UK tranche in ours.
requests.why: The UK has invited this trade and EU exporters hold 3.6Mt of access into the UK market. A reciprocal predictability package could settle both processes at once and give the Council a defensible political narrative, but I need to know whether Brussels will countenance cross-process linkage.

private_rationale: The UK's opening is a classic anchor at historic trade levels — they will expect to be beaten down and have clearly left themselves room. Their real tells are the red lines: country-specific allocation (genuine), the FTA disapplication (genuine and dangerous, given the Japan/Korea whisperings), and the implicit threat embedded in the 'balance' language on their own measure — they are signalling they can squeeze 3.6Mt of EU export access if we squeeze their 2.4Mt. My priority this round is to lock in the cooperative frame and the linkage possibility before positions harden. I have slightly overstated nothing to Brussels: I genuinely cannot move on volume without a mandate, and the worst outcome is not a tough negotiation but a failed one that ends in a joint FTA dispute, retaliatory withdrawals, and a poisoned Geneva working relationship I have to live with for years. instruction: Good round. You were right to hold on volume and right to bank the cheap concessions early. Here is your Round 2 mandate. Open by converting your signalled flexibility into a concrete counter: accept country-specific allocation in principle — it is their red line and costs us little against a global FCFS pool we could not administer cleanly anyway. Table a total pool of 1.5 million tonnes with a UK-specific tranche of 900,000 tonnes, licensed with quarterly releases — accept their administration ask in full, it is free and it buys goodwill. Hold the out-of-quota rate at 50% but signal movement: you may indicate 40% as where we could land, framed as recognition of their principal supplying interest. Offer five-year duration with a genuine review clause now — bank it. Do not concede anything further on volume in Round 2 beyond the above; if they press, you have headroom to a UK tranche of 1.2Mt within a total of 2.0Mt, but that is your Round 3/4 fallback ladder, not your Round 2 position — sequence it: tranche movement first, total pool movement last. On the FTA disapplication: do not concede a carve-out yet, but you may say we are prepared to resolve it within the package — explore options such as conditional or deferred application tied to quota operation — and make clear any resolution is linked to the reciprocal access discussion. On linkage: formally propose that both processes move together — continued country-specific access for EU exporters under the UK measure (they hold 3.6Mt into us and our exporters need that predictability) in exchange for the UK tranche. Frame the whole as a mutual predictability package both sides can defend domestically. Keep the tone warm, keep momentum, but make no commitments beyond this authority.

authority.notes: Fallback ladder, not to be tabled in Round 2: Round 3 may move UK tranche to 1.05Mt; Round 4 maximum is UK tranche 1.2Mt within a total pool of 2.0Mt. Out-of-quota rate floor is 40%; 35% is an absolute final concession only if it closes the deal AND is tied to resolution of the FTA disapplication and confirmed reciprocal access for EU exporters into the UK. Any FTA carve-out or conditional/deferred disapplication for the UK requires reciprocal commitments and must be flagged to me before being given — Korea and Japan will claim equivalent treatment and I need to manage that in the Council. Licensing with quarterly releases is accepted. Country-specific allocation is accepted in principle.

private_rationale: I need a deal before June without handing the steel-producing member states a hollow measure. The UK's 2.4Mt ask equals their historic trade — accepting anything near it makes the modification pointless and the Council will not vote it. But a 400kt global pool is indefensible against a principal supplying interest holding 2.4Mt of trade, and no-deal costs us the June vote and invites US retaliation on top. The cheap concessions (country-specific allocation, licensing, quarterly releases, review clause) cost us nothing in protection and buy the architecture the UK needs politically. The real currency is the reciprocal access linkage — 3.6Mt of EU exports into the UK dwarfs what we are conceding — and the FTA disapplication, which I am holding as the closing card. My fallback ladder gets the UK to roughly half their ask; if they will not move off 2.4Mt by Round 3, I will need to decide whether the Council accepts a larger UK tranche framed as transitional, or whether we run the no-deal risk.

report: Round 1 opened constructively. The EU confirmed the modification itself is settled in Brussels, but flagged genuine flexibility on: allocation method (open in principle to country-specific shares), administration (licensing discussable), and duration/review (offered a review clause from the start as good faith). They deliberately held back on volume and product coverage, saying they were 'listening before they speak' — an invitation for us to anchor first. They proposed treating FTA disapplication as part of the package rather than a threshold issue, and floated linkage between this negotiation and our own Article XXVIII/steel measure, where EU exporters hold country-specific allocations. I tabled a concrete opening: 6Mt total pool, 2.4Mt UK-specific tranche (anchored to the historic reference period), 25% out-of-quota rate, five years with review, quarterly-released licensed tranches, and made clear that a small quota share plus FTA disapplication is not a conclusion we can take to you — and that consequences would not stay contained to steel. I signalled willingness to discuss EU treatment under our measure as part of a balanced outcome. No numbers were countered by the EU; the real negotiation on volume starts in Round 2. Their June Council deadline gives us leverage if we keep momentum, but they clearly intend to settle and have room to move on architecture.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU has already conceded the two structural points that matter most in principle — country-specific allocation and a review clause — and has not yet defended the 400,000 tonne volume or the 50% rate. Accepting anything now would lock in our opening before the EU has shown its hand on volume, which is where the real value is. Walking away is untenable: no-deal means the notified 400,000t global FCFS pool, which is the worst-case outcome for UK industry, and our retaliation cannot bite for six months. Continuing costs us nothing and the EU's June deadline means each round increases pressure on them, not us.

instruction: Well handled — anchoring first on volume was right, and their silence on numbers confirms volume is where the negotiation lives. For Round 2, hold your opening architecture (country-specific UK tranche, quarterly licensed releases, review clause) and do not move on any number until the Commission tables a volume. When they do, you may negotiate within this envelope: UK tranche floor 1.6 million tonnes, target remains 2.4Mt — open every exchange by defending 2.4Mt on the reference-period basis and concede only in return for named EU movement, not goodwill. Out-of-quota rate: hold at 25%, hard ceiling 30%. Duration: you may offer up to 7 years (from 5) as a low-cost early concession — they want permanence, and this is cheap for us given the review clause; use it to buy volume. Review clause is mandatory in any settlement. On the linkage to our own safeguard: you are authorised to offer improved country-specific quota allocations for EU exporters under our measure, but only explicitly conditioned on the UK tranche landing at or above 2.0Mt — present it as a conditional package, not a concession, and give no tonnage figures on our side until they have moved on volume. On FTA disapplication: hold the line that it must be withdrawn or, at minimum, time-limited to the TRQ duration with TCA treatment restored thereafter; you may signal that full restoration would unlock UK flexibility on total pool and duration, but do not trade it for quota volume alone — restored TCA terms are worth more than tonnage because they cover out-of-quota trade, and the EU knows it. On Korea and Japan: do not join any joint FTA dispute initiative, but you may let it be known, without commitment, that several members are discussing coordinated responses and that a satisfactory bilateral architecture here would take the heat out of that. Keep momentum: close Round 2 by proposing a drafting exchange on administration (quarterly licensing) and review clause text, so we bank the architecture while volume is fought over. Your walk-away floor, for your own calibration: a guaranteed UK tranche below 1.6Mt with FTA disapplication intact is worse than no-deal plus retaliation, and you should make clear, politely, that you cannot recommend such a package to London.

authority.notes: Figures are floors/ceilings, not opening positions — opening positions remain 2.4Mt UK tranche, 25% out-of-quota. Review clause is a hard requirement. Country-specific allocation with quarterly licensed tranche releases is a hard requirement. UK safeguard improvements for EU exporters may be offered only conditional on UK tranche >= 2.0Mt. FTA disapplication must be withdrawn or time-limited to TRQ duration with TCA restoration thereafter; not tradeable for quota volume alone. Any settlement below 1.6Mt UK tranche or above 30% out-of-quota must be referred back before agreement.

private_rationale: The floor of 1.6Mt is uncomfortable but defensible: two plants are on the brink, and a guaranteed country-specific 1.6Mt at 25-30% out-of-quota, plus restored or time-limited TCA treatment, keeps roughly two-thirds of current EU access predictable — probably enough, combined with the Minister's subsidisation option, to keep the owners at the table. My real target is 2.0Mt+, which triggers the safeguard linkage and gives us a genuinely saleable deal. The EU's June deadline and their eagerness to settle ('no reason to look beyond this negotiation for remedies') suggest they fear unravelling via retaliation and the Korea/Japan track more than we fear no-deal — but I must not test that bluff past Round 3, because our no-deal outcome is catastrophic and retaliation cannot bite for six months. Duration is my cheapest currency: they want permanence, and 7 years plus a review clause costs us little. FTA restoration is the highest-value item in play and I have protected it accordingly. If Round 2 produces no EU volume number, I will need to consider whether the Commission is slow-walking toward their June cliff-edge to compress our options — in which case the Korea/Japan lever becomes more attractive.

public_message: Thank you for a concrete and candid opening — that is exactly what moves a negotiation, and I want to respond in kind. You asked where we see headroom, so let me give you substance rather than principles. First, on the architecture: we accept country-specific allocation. You were clear it is a red line, and we have heard you — a global first-come pool will not feature in the landing zone. We also accept your administration proposal in full: licensing, with quarterly tranche releases so shares cannot be front-loaded or stranded. Second, duration: we offer five years with a genuine review clause, now, as a firm commitment rather than a possibility. Third, volume — and here I will be honest with you, as you were with me. We cannot go anywhere near 6 million tonnes or a 2.4 million tonne tranche; figures at that scale do not modify the measure, they negate it, and no Council would conclude on that basis. What I can put on the table today is a total pool of 1.5 million tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 900,000 tonnes. I recognise that is well short of your historic trade. I would ask you to read it as a first figure from our side, tabled in good faith in response to yours, not as a final position. Fourth, the out-of-quota rate: I am not in a position to move to 25% — that is outside any zone I can see — but I can tell you today that 50% is not where we expect to land, and that a rate around 40% is within the realm of the possible as recognition of your principal supplying interest. Fifth, the FTA interaction. I have heard that this is conclusion-blocking for you if left standing alongside a small quota. We are prepared to resolve it within this package — options such as conditional or deferred application tied to the operation of the quota are ones we can genuinely explore — but resolution on that front is linked, in our minds, to the sixth point. You put your own measure on the table, and I welcome that. I would propose we formalise the linkage: continued country-specific access for EU exporters under your steel measure — where they currently hold 3.6 million tonnes of predictable access into your market — as the counterpart to the UK tranche in ours. Taken together, that is a mutual predictability package: your producers know what they hold into the EU, ours know what they hold into the UK, and both of us can defend the outcome at home. That is also, I would suggest, the kind of package that gives neither of us a reason to look elsewhere for remedies — and gives nobody else a reason to invite you to. I look forward to your reaction.

private_rationale: This executes the Brussels mandate exactly: convert the signalled flexibilities (country-specific allocation, licensing with quarterly releases, five years plus review) into banked concessions at zero cost, table the authorised first figures (1.5Mt pool / 900kt tranche), and signal — without committing — the 40% rate landing zone to keep the UK invested on volume rather than rate. The 900kt figure is deliberately low relative to the fallback ladder (1.05Mt then 1.2Mt within 2.0Mt) to preserve negotiating room across Rounds 3 and 4, and it is framed explicitly as a first figure so the UK reads movement rather than intransigence. The reciprocal linkage is now formally proposed, which serves three purposes: it gives the Council a defensible political narrative, it creates the hook for resolving the FTA disapplication later (Brussels requires reciprocal commitments for any carve-out), and it converts the UK's latent threat over its own measure into a shared interest in settlement. Hinting that the package forecloses 'looking elsewhere for remedies' addresses the Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk without naming it. Nothing beyond the authority has been committed: rate floor held at 40%, no FTA carve-out conceded, fallback volumes untouched.

public_message: Thank you — that was a substantive response and I want to recognise it as such. Let me bank what we have agreed before I turn to where we remain apart, because it is not nothing: country-specific allocation is settled; licensing with quarterly tranche releases is settled; five years with a genuine review clause is settled as a firm commitment. That is the architecture we asked for, and I will report to London that the Commission has moved seriously. To lock it in, I propose we instruct our teams to begin a drafting exchange on the administration and review clause text this week, so the agreed structure is on paper while we fight over the numbers. Now, the numbers. I will be as honest with you as you were with me: a 900,000 tonne tranche is not a first figure I can work with — it is 37% of our historic trade on the very reference period the WTO uses to establish the interest you have accepted we hold, and it would leave the majority of UK production without a market. I cannot take a figure in that range to London as anything other than a rejection. But you have moved on structure, and momentum deserves momentum, so let me move too. On total pool, I come down from 6 million to 4.5 million tonnes — a significant contraction, offered in direct response to your acceptance of the architecture. On duration, I can offer seven years rather than five, with the review clause intact — that gives your domestic industry a longer horizon of certainty, and I offer it explicitly to buy volume, not as a gift. My tranche figure remains 2.4 million tonnes, and the out-of-quota rate remains 25% — I note you said 50% is not where you expect to land, and I would encourage you to test 40% against your Council harder, because the rate determines whether out-of-quota trade is possible at all, and for the UK the tranche plus the rate together define the outcome, not the tranche alone. On the FTA point and the linkage you propose: I can confirm there is a package here. Continued predictable, country-specific access for EU exporters under our measure is something I am authorised to discuss — but I want to be transparent that such a package only becomes possible for me if the UK tranche lands at or above 2 million tonnes. Below that, there is no balanced outcome to sell at home, and the linkage you want cannot be built. On the FTA disapplication itself, resolution means withdrawal or, at minimum, time-limitation to the TRQ period with TCA treatment restored thereafter — I would observe that restoring TCA terms is worth a great deal to us precisely because it governs out-of-quota trade, and a clean resolution there would unlock further flexibility from us on pool size and duration. Finally, since you raised looking elsewhere for remedies: I would rather neither of us did. I should say, without any commitment from my side, that I am not the only delegation in this building being pressed toward coordinated responses, and a satisfactory bilateral architecture here takes the heat out of that for everyone. Let us use the next round to close the distance on volume.

public_message: Thank you, colleague. Let me start where you started, because you are right that banking agreements is how this ends. The drafting exchange is agreed and my team will have administration and review text with yours this week. Duration at seven years is banked, and I note for the record that you accepted it explicitly against movement on tonnage — I intend to honour that bargain, and this round I will show you how. On your volume move: I recognise a second consecutive move when I see one, and I will report it to London as such. But I must be honest in return: 1.05 million tonnes is 44% of the reference-period trade on which my principal supplying interest rests, and it does not become defensible in London by being defended hard in Brussels. However — you asked which lines matter, and that is the most useful question put to me in this negotiation, so let me answer it concretely rather than rhetorically. The UK interest is concentrated in hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod. I am prepared to engage seriously on guaranteed product-specific sub-tranches within the UK tranche on those lines, with quarterly licensing applied per line, at full tonnage value against the UK share. If that track is real, it changes the arithmetic of this negotiation, because it means effective access can be built line by line rather than fought over as a single headline. Let me then respond to your call for reciprocal movement, and I will do it as one package, because partial credit does not close this. If the UK tranche — headline plus product sub-tranches — lands at or above 2 million tonnes, then three things happen together: my total pool ask comes down from 4.5 million tonnes toward the region of 3 million, which substantially eases your Turkey and Korea problem; my rate position can move from 25% toward the high twenties as part of the final package; and I can put concrete tonnage on the table for EU exporters under our own measure — continuation of your existing country-specific allocations with a staged uplift of up to ten percent above current volumes. I name that figure today so that your Round 4 instructions can be written against a complete package, not a fragment. On the rate, I hear your candour and I will be candid back: 40% is not a number I can commend, and the rate conversation is not settled — but I have just shown you the conditions under which I move, and they are now entirely within your gift. On the FTA point: time-limitation with restoration thereafter means objective, automatic triggers and automatic restoration of TCA treatment at TRQ expiry. I say this plainly, with respect: anything discretionary — anything subject to review, renewal or further decision — is permanent disapplication by another name, and London will read it as such. Finally, on the calendar: I agree Round 4 should close. The package that closes it is now on this table in full: a UK tranche at or above 2 million tonnes built from headline and product-line guarantees, an out-of-quota rate at or below 30%, seven years, a genuine review clause, quarterly licensing, automatic TCA restoration at expiry, and reciprocal predictability for your exporters under our measure. Every element of that is movement I have offered against movement you control. I look forward to your final position.

report: Round 3 produced the UK's first complete closing package and real movement on every element except the one that matters most to us. Banked and now locked: country-specific allocation, licensing with quarterly releases, seven-year duration (accepted by me explicitly against tonnage movement), genuine review clause, and the drafting exchange — UK text arrives this week. I tabled our Round 3 position (pool 1.75Mt, UK tranche 1.05Mt, 40% stated as the Council's edge, FTA time-limitation framed as explorable with stated conditions) and opened the product-line track. The UK seized the product track immediately and concretely: their interest is concentrated in hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod, and they proposed guaranteed product-specific sub-tranches within the UK tranche on those lines, with per-line quarterly licensing at full tonnage value. They then tabled a conditional package: if the UK tranche — headline plus product sub-tranches — reaches 2Mt, their total pool ask falls from 4.5Mt to ~3Mt (materially easing our Turkey/Korea exposure), their rate position moves from 25% to the high twenties, and they put concrete tonnage on the table for EU exporters under their measure: continuation of our existing country-specific allocations plus a staged uplift of up to 10% above current volumes (i.e. up to ~3.96Mt of predictable EU access). On the FTA they hardened one point: time-limitation must mean objective, automatic triggers and automatic TCA restoration at TRQ expiry — anything discretionary will be read in London as permanent disapplication. Their stated Round 4 closing package: UK tranche at or above 2Mt, out-of-quota rate at or below 30%, seven years, review clause, quarterly licensing, automatic TCA restoration, reciprocal predictability for EU exporters. The core problem is unchanged and now explicit: their linkage threshold (2Mt) sits 650,000 tonnes above my Round 4 hard ceiling (1.35Mt), and their rate ceiling (30%) sits 5 points below my absolute floor (35%). Both sides agree Round 4 closes or the process drifts past June.

The product sub-tranche track is the one genuine bridge: if we structure generous guaranteed sub-tranches on HRC, plate, rebar and wire rod at full tonnage value within a 1.35Mt tranche, effective UK access on the lines that actually matter approaches their historic trade composition even though the headline figure does not — and the UK themselves framed the 2Mt threshold as 'headline plus product sub-tranches', which may give us definitional room to count sub-tranche guarantees toward it. For Round 4 I propose tabling maximum volume authority (1.35Mt/2.2Mt) with the sub-tranche architecture fully specified, the FTA time-limitation finally tabled with automatic restoration triggers, conditional on written confirmation of the reciprocal access uplift, and holding 40% with 35% deployed only as the closing concession. instruction: Round 4 closes or we drift past June — treat this as the endgame and table the package as a single whole, not as fragments they can pick apart. Sequence it as follows. First, open by tabling the FTA resolution, now formally on the table: disapplication limited strictly to the TRQ period, with objective automatic triggers and automatic restoration of TCA treatment at expiry — no review, no renewal, no discretion. Say plainly we have accepted their formulation in full. State its condition in the same breath: written confirmation, in this process, of the reciprocal access package for EU exporters — continuation of our existing country-specific allocations in full, plus the staged uplift locked at 10% with a binding schedule and duration matched to ours. Do not let the FTA point float free of that condition for a single intervention. Second, volume: table the total pool at 2.2 million tonnes and the UK tranche at 1.35 million tonnes, and then immediately build the construction their own framing allows. They defined their 2 million tonne threshold as 'headline plus product sub-tranches' — take them at their word. Within the UK tranche, guarantee binding sub-tranche minima on hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod summing to no less than 1.1 million tonnes, licensed quarterly per line with intra-year carry-over of unused tonnage. On top of the tranche, offer a UK-priority residual mechanism: first call, ahead of any other origin, on up to 550,000 tonnes of residual or unused pool tonnage on those four lines. Present this accurately and confidently: guaranteed UK access of 1.35 million tonnes with effective access of up to 1.9 million tonnes on the lines where their industry actually trades — against historic trade of 2.4 million concentrated on exactly those lines. That is a package London can defend, and you should say so. Third, rate: open at 40% and hold it through their first response. If — and only if — they move materially off both 2 million tonnes and 30%, you may move to 35% as the final rate, deployed against written reciprocal confirmation. 35% is the floor; there is nothing below it, and you should say that once, calmly, at the end. Fourth, duration: if they accept a headline tranche below 2 million tonnes, offer the eighth year explicitly against that acceptance — duration is our cheapest currency and they have already shown they price it. Finally, tone: warm, complete, and terminal. Make clear this is the full extent of what the Commission can defend to the Council, that every element they asked for is either granted or answered with a construction, and that what remains is a decision for London, not a negotiation for Geneva.

The strongest reasons to close: the reciprocal package locks up to ~3.96Mt of EU export access into the UK, kills the UK retaliation track that lands six months after a no-deal, defuses the Japan/Korea joint FTA dispute via the automatic-restoration formulation, and gets the measure to the Council by June — against a backdrop of US tariff threats we do not need compounding. The strongest reason the package might still fail is the rate, where I have refused to move below 35%: a 30% rate on sensitive lines would leak MFN and gut the regime for the member states who must vote for it. If London cannot take effective access of ~1.9Mt on their actual trade lines, automatic TCA restoration, 35%, eight years and a confirmed reciprocal uplift, then no package this side of negating the measure was ever available, and proceeding as notified with a documented record of good-faith negotiation is the least-bad position. report: Round 3 banked more architecture but left the core gap wide. The EU formally agreed to begin the drafting exchange on administration/review text this week and accepted seven years expressly against tonnage movement. It then made a second volume move: total pool 1.75Mt and UK tranche 1.05Mt, while warning that one-sided movement cannot continue and that 1.05Mt should be read as defended ground rather than a waypoint to 2Mt. It hardened on rate: 25% impossible, 40% at the very edge of Council tolerance, and sought to treat the rate as effectively settled at 40. It kept FTA resolution in play only as part of a final package, conditional on confirmed reciprocal access for EU exporters under our measure and substantial movement of our tranche ask toward its zone. Most usefully, it opened a product-specific track and asked which of the 41 lines matter, indicating scope to do considerably more on concentrated UK-interest lines than the headline tranche implies. I answered with hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod, and put the full closing package on the table: if UK effective tranche reaches >=2.0Mt via headline plus guaranteed quarterly-licensed line sub-tranches, our pool ask falls toward ~3Mt, rate can move toward the high twenties only in the final package, and EU exporters keep existing country-specific allocations under our measure with a staged uplift up to 10%. I restated that FTA drafting must have objective automatic triggers and automatic TCA restoration at expiry; anything discretionary is permanent disapplication by another name. Round 4 is now the endgame.

recommendation.reasoning: The terms currently tabled by the EU are outside authority on both tonnage and rate: 1.05Mt is below the 1.6Mt floor and 40% is above the 30% ceiling, so acceptance is impossible and referral would be required even if we wanted to close. Walking away is worse: no-deal leaves the notified 400,000t global first-come pool and our retaliation cannot bite for six months. The EU has, however, conceded allocation, licensing, quarterly release, seven years and review in principle, has moved twice on volume, faces the June Council date, and has now invited a product-line route that could convert an unacceptable headline into acceptable effective access. The right course is to make Round 4 a single final package exchange: no partial concessions, movement only if EU puts line-guaranteed tonnage, rate at/below 30 and automatic TCA restoration on the table together.

instruction: Round 4 is the closing round. Open by confirming that the administration/review drafting exchange is under way and that country-specific allocation, quarterly licensing and seven years are banked. Do not make further unilateral concessions. Present a single final-package proposition, making clear that no element is agreed unless all elements are agreed. Begin with an effective UK tranche of 2.2 million tonnes, comprising guaranteed product sub-tranches, and an out-of-quota rate of 28%, with the UK excluded from the FTA-disapplication provision so that TCA treatment continues. If necessary, close at an effective UK tranche of at least 2.0 million tonnes, rate no higher than 30%, seven years, a genuine review clause, quarterly licensing and full FTA resolution. In that band you may confirm continuation of EU exporters' existing country-specific allocations under our measure and offer a staged uplift of up to 10%, strictly conditional on the whole package being implemented. You are also authorised, as the minimum acceptable outcome, to accept an effective UK tranche between 1.6 and 2.0 million tonnes only if every tonne is underwritten by guaranteed quarterly-licensed sub-tranches on hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod; the rate is no more than 30%; duration is seven years; the review clause cannot unilaterally reduce UK access; and FTA disapplication is either withdrawn or automatically expires with TCA treatment restored without further decision. In that band, confirm continuation of existing EU allocations only as part of the final package and offer no uplift. Product floors are: hot-rolled coil 700000 tonnes, plate 350000 tonnes, rebar 300000 tonnes and wire rod 250000 tonnes, totalling 1.6 million tonnes. For a 2.0 million-tonne outcome seek hot-rolled coil 850000, plate 450000, rebar 400000 and wire rod 300000. You may vary individual lines by no more than 5% only if the aggregate floor is maintained and no line falls below 90% of its floor. Require equal quarterly releases by line, automatic carry-forward of unused quantities within the year, and no reallocation outside the UK tranche before a final-quarter UK application window has closed; any end-year reallocation must cover only genuinely unclaimed quantities and must not prejudice the following year's UK tranche. The review must examine volume, allocation, rate, product mix and market conditions, but cannot itself reduce the tranche, alter the product guarantees or raise the rate; any adverse modification requires agreement and fresh compensation. On FTA drafting, seek complete UK exclusion first. Failing that, conditional or deferred disapplication is acceptable only with objective automatic triggers, a fixed expiry coterminous with the TRQ and automatic restoration of TCA treatment. Reject discretionary renewal, review-based continuation, political triggers or wording requiring a further EU act to restore TCA treatment. Anti-circumvention provisions may be accepted only if they are evidence-based, proportionate, non-retroactive and subject to consultation and objective review; reject any discretionary power to suspend or reduce UK access. Continue to decline coordination with Japan and Korea, while stating neutrally that a satisfactory bilateral outcome would reduce pressure for broader coordinated responses. If the EU cannot meet the minimum package, do not settle. State that you cannot recommend it to London, reserve all UK rights under Article XXVIII and leave the table on terms that preserve our retaliation and coalition options.

authority.notes: The UK tranche figure is a hard effective-access floor, not merely a headline figure. Every tonne must be guaranteed through country-specific, product-specific, quarterly-licensed sub-tranches. Product floors: hot-rolled coil 700000 tonnes, plate 350000 tonnes, rebar 300000 tonnes, wire rod 250000 tonnes. Aggregate below 1.6 million tonnes, an out-of-quota rate above 30%, duration below seven years, or absence of a genuine review clause cannot be accepted. The review must not permit unilateral deterioration of UK access. FTA disapplication must be withdrawn for the UK or automatically expire with TCA treatment restored without discretion or a further EU decision. At 1.6 million to below 2.0 million tonnes, existing EU allocations under the UK safeguard may be continued as part of a complete compliant package, but no uplift may be offered. At 2.0 million tonnes or more, a staged uplift of up to 10% may be offered, subject to implementation of the full EU package and reciprocal snapback if the EU reduces access, breaches the FTA sunset or suspends the arrangement. The total pool is not itself a UK settlement metric, but do not accept any pool drafting that dilutes or competes with the guaranteed UK sub-tranches.

However, the architecture is substantially agreed and Round 4 offers a credible route to closure through the authorised package: a larger UK tranche, binding product sub-tranches and priority residual access on key lines, automatic TCA restoration after the TRQ period, and reciprocal access commitments for EU exporters. The EU's current position — a 1.05Mt UK tranche against 1.75Mt total pool, 40% out-of-quota rate, and FTA resolution still only conditional and uncommitted — is outside every element of my settlement authority: the tranche is below the 1.6Mt hard floor, the rate is above the 30% hard ceiling, and no acceptable FTA drafting exists yet. I cannot accept, and cannot even refer such a package for acceptance. Equally, accepting the default is untenable: the notified outcome (400,000t global first-come pool, 50% rate, no review) is the worst-case scenario for UK industry and our retaliation cannot bite for six months, by which point two plants may already have closed. There is genuine momentum worth preserving: the EU has banked country-specific allocation, quarterly licensing, seven years and a review clause, has moved twice on volume, has opened a product-specific sub-tranche track that London's Round 4 authority is specifically designed to exploit, and faces a hard June Council deadline that concentrates its mind, not ours. The correct course is to continue into Round 4 and present the single final-package proposition as instructed — effective UK tranche of 2.2Mt built from guaranteed quarterly-licensed line sub-tranches, 28% rate, UK exclusion from FTA disapplication, closing at no less than 1.6Mt fully underwritten line-by-line, 30%, seven years, genuine review, and automatic TCA restoration — with the safeguard continuation and, at 2.0Mt or above, the 10% uplift as the reciprocal lever. public_message: Thank you, colleague. You asked for a final position against a complete package, and that is what I will give you — tabled as a single whole, because the elements only hold together. Let me take them in turn. First, the FTA interaction, because you told us plainly what resolution means and I want you to hear that we heard you. The disapplication of FTA treatment for UK-origin steel will be limited strictly to the life of this TRQ. It will operate through objective, automatic triggers, and TCA treatment will be restored automatically at TRQ expiry. There is no review, no renewal, no discretion. We have accepted your formulation in full, and I am tabling it as agreed text, not as an exploration. Its condition, stated in the same breath so there is no ambiguity: written confirmation in this process of the reciprocal access package for EU exporters under your measure — continuation of our existing country-specific allocations in full, plus the staged uplift locked at ten percent with a binding schedule, duration matched to ours. Second, volume. The total pool is 2.2 million tonnes. The UK-specific tranche is 1.35 million tonnes — a fifty percent increase on where we began, and I will be honest that it is at the outer limit of what any Commission can defend to this Council. But you defined your threshold as headline plus product sub-tranches, and I take you at your word. Within that tranche, we guarantee binding sub-tranche minima on hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar and wire rod summing to no less than 1.1 million tonnes, licensed quarterly per line, with intra-year carry-over of unused tonnage. And on top of the tranche, we offer a UK-priority residual mechanism: first call, ahead of any other origin, on up to 550,000 tonnes of residual or unused pool tonnage on those four lines. State it accurately and it is this: guaranteed UK access of 1.35 million tonnes, with effective access of up to 1.9 million tonnes on precisely the lines where your industry trades, against historic trade of 2.4 million concentrated on those same lines. That is a package London can defend, and I believe you know it. Third, the rate: 40%. I have told you it is at the edge of what the Council can accept, and it remains there today. Fourth, everything we have already banked stands: country-specific allocation, quarterly licensing, the genuine review clause, seven years, and the drafting text our teams are exchanging this week. Colleague, this is the full extent of what the Commission can defend. Every element you asked for is either granted or answered with a construction. You told me last round that a satisfactory bilateral architecture takes the heat out of other pressures in this building — this is that architecture. What remains now is not a negotiation for Geneva but a decision for London.

I followed the sequence exactly: the FTA time-limitation on the UK's own terms is the biggest single concession and leading with it maximises its weight while its condition (written reciprocal confirmation with 10% uplift locked) is stated inseparably in the same breath, per instructions.
